transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-02
Time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Ruiz (HelixAI - Head ML Infra), Sara Kim (HelixAI - Sr ML Eng), Tom Larsen (CTO)

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we're planning to focus on model-level tuning, runtime knobs, and specific tradeoffs for Llama, Mistral, and Qwen, and also hit MoE routing and RoPE scaling. can we do a quick round robin intro?
[00:18] Daniel Ruiz: yeah daniel here, we run a mix of on-prem A100 clusters and some H100 cloud spares, looking to push longer contexts for our research product, late 2026-ish rollout.
[00:28] Sara Kim: sara, i manage inference pipelines - key constraints are latency SLO 150ms p95 for 512 tokens and cost target per 1k tokens.
[00:34] Tom Larsen: tom, product-wise we need predictable tail latency and privacy (VPC/on prem).
[00:40] Maya Patel: great, thanks. quick agenda: kernel selection and batching, KV cache behavior for long vs short contexts, quantization impacts on quality and perf, moE routing cost math, roPE scaling options, and recommended Redwood runtime profiles.

[02:05] Alex Chen: starting with kernel selection: on Llama-style models CPU/GPU kernel choices and fused attention matter - for H100 we pick the optimized attention kernels in the runtime, for Mistral smaller heads and wider ff make different memory patterns. so throughput numbers will vary.
[02:40] Sara Kim: one practical q - if we go 4-bit quant vs 8-bit, what's the expected perf delta and when does quality suffer?
[02:48] Maya Patel: uh good question. in our tests 8-bit (normal q8) gives roughly 1.6-1.8x throughput vs fp16 on same hw, and 4-bit INT4/QLoRA-ish can be 2.5-3x but with more variance in quality depending on model family. Mistral tends to be more robust to aggressive quant because of its activation distributions, while Qwen sometimes shows hallucination drift at lower precision for instruction-following tasks.
[03:20] Daniel Ruiz: are those numbers with batching enabled? what's the batch size baseline?
[03:25] Maya Patel: baseline was batch 4 for generation with sequence 512 and continuous KV caching warm. throughput scales with batch up to kernel saturation; for latency-sensitive SLOs, batch 1-2 with continuous batching windows of ~20-50ms is typical.

[06:10] Speaker 1: (inaudible) kernel selection yeah

[07:00] Alex Chen: on KV cache: two modes matter - prefix / session caching and full KV reuse. warm cache reduces decoder compute dramatically because attention keys/values are reused. cold starts are the killer. for long context workloads we recommend aggressive prefix caching and segmenting prompts so you can chunk and reuse.
[07:35] Sara Kim: when you say reuse, do you still cache per-token KV or are you doing keyed snapshots?
[07:42] Maya Patel: it's per layer per token but we store snapshots for sessions; in Redwood runtime we also support partial cache eviction to free memory for high-req customers. some transcription systems mishear KV as 'KV cash' so that's a caveat, ha.

[09:20] Tom Larsen: okay, for MoE - we've toyed with Switch Transformer style models. the routing overhead was large, what's the cost model?
[09:30] Maya Patel: MoE routing cost has two pieces: the gating/route compute (small) and the overhead of shuffling activations across experts (memory + bandwidth). for single-node GPUs, if experts are colocated you can limit cross-device traffic; but with large expert counts the activation memory and all-reduce style ops add latency. net effect: MoE can reduce FLOPs for the dense path but increase wall-clock latency and memory pressure if not carefully mapped.
[10:05] Daniel Ruiz: any rule of thumb for when MoE pays off?
[10:10] Maya Patel: usually MoE helps when model size for quality is pushing multi-100B dense and you can afford higher variance in per-request latency; for strict p95 latency targets it's often trickier unless you dedicate capacity and tune routing thresholds.

[12:45] Alex Chen: onto RoPE scaling: long-context extrapolation is sensitive to how positional embeddings are handled. Llama-style RoPE can degrade for very long sequences. we talked about linear RoPE scaling (scale factor) and sliding windows. practical approach: either (1) apply RoPE scaling factors with careful re-normalization at inference time, or (2) implement chunked attention with stateful KV cache and position rebase on the server side.
[13:30] Sara Kim: what about changing model weights to support longer RoPE? is that needed?
[13:35] Maya Patel: sometimes you need a small finetune or LoRA-like adapter to stabilize, especially for Qwen variants. Mistral often requires less retuning due to its internal positional biases. but for production you can do server-side fixes first.

[15:12] Alex Chen: benchmark note - cold-cache token throughput can be 30-50% worse than warm cache for 2k contexts on H100 when you include KV materialization. you should plan for that in autoscaling policies.
[15:45] Daniel Ruiz: how do you recommend autoscaling to account for cold start spikes?
[15:50] Maya Patel: we suggest a combination: (a) reserve a small warm pool for high-tier customers, (b) predictive pre-warming based on request patterns, and (c) fallback to smaller but cheaper model variant if latency SLOs threatened. Redwood routing can split traffic by policy.

[18:22] Tom Larsen: security questions - VPC and KMS for private deployment, can Redwood integrate with our HSM?
[18:28] Alex Chen: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. we'll share the integration doc after call.

[20:00] Sara Kim: back to batching - you mentioned continuous batching - how does that interact with strict latency SLOs?
[20:10] Maya Patel: continuous batching is micro-batching where we aggregate requests for 10-50ms windows. it slightly increases mean latency but can drastically improve throughput. for tight p95 you reduce the window and use prioritized routing for small requests. also kernel-level fused ops can reduce per-token overhead with bigger micro-batches.

[22:40] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) sorry

[24:05] Alex Chen: another practical tip on quantization and evals: always keep a small eval set of your production prompts. q4 might be fine for intents and retrieval augmentation, but q4 can degrade instruction-following in Qwen family. track metrics and use Redwood Optimize to recommend which layers to keep in higher precision.

[27:30] Daniel Ruiz: runtime knobs - you mentioned kernel selection based on seq len; can the runtime switch kernels mid-session?
[27:38] Maya Patel: yes, runtime can pick kernels per request but switching mid-generation is costly; we tend to pick kernels per-route. for mixed request distributions we recommend separate routes for short vs long context so kernels remain stable.

[31:10] Sara Kim: memory considerations - with RoPE rebase and long KV, we hit memory limits on 80GB GPUs. what are options?
[31:20] Maya Patel: options: quantize model weights to reduce model memory, shard KV across devices (adds interconnect latency), use sequence chunking + disk-backed checkpointing for very long sessions, or move to larger instances with more RAM. also choose model variants that have lower per-token KV size (fewer heads or smaller hidden dims).

[35:00] Alex Chen: example config we recommend for HelixAI use-case: H100 instances, q8 for Mistral and Llama, conservative q4 for Qwen on non-critical paths, batch window 20ms for general traffic, reserve 2-4 warm GPUs per service to mitigate cold-cache.

[37:15] Tom Larsen: how about model fallbacks - can Redwood auto-fallback to a cheaper variant on overload?
[37:22] Maya Patel: yes, routing policies allow automatic fallback to pinned smaller model variants or hosted instances with different SLAs. it keeps requests alive with degraded quality vs outage.

[40:45] Daniel Ruiz: for MoE again - any profiling tips to measure routing overhead?

[40:52] Maya Patel: measure three metrics: gate compute time, expert shuffle time (network+copy), and per-expert activation memory. our tracing hooks in console can break down per-token cost by these phases. we can share a profiling deck.

[44:00] Alex Chen: quick note on quantization-per-layer: keep attention and ln in fp16 usually, quantize FFN dense layers first; that's where most gains are. also watch out for operator-level fidelity - some kernels still experimental.

[46:20] Speaker 3 (maybe Transcriber): (background)

[48:10] Sara Kim: final question on RoPE: for long generation, do you rebase positions or use relative pos?
[48:18] Maya Patel: rebase is simpler for server-side stateful generation - you reassign token positions relative to a sliding window. relative pos embeddings require model support. for backward compatibility rebase + KV snapshots is practical.

[51:05] Alex Chen: ok let's recap next steps: we'll run the benchmark Maya mentioned, share quantization guide and security/KMS integration doc, and propose a follow-up demo around mid-April.
[51:25] Daniel Ruiz: thanks, that sounds good.
[51:30] Tom Larsen: appreciate it, please also include cost estimates for reserved warm pool.
[51:35] Alex Chen: will do.

[61:00] Alex Chen: thanks everyone, end call.
